extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comedy writers, students and scholars of literary/theatre theory
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical account of the principal methods that produce the comic (for plots, situations, characters, and language), with examples and guidance on how and why each method produces laughter. Useful for writers and analysts seeking concrete devices and their conditions of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation (a combination of circumstances) recurs several times in its original form and thus contrasts with the changing stream of life; repetition produces the comic by reproducing the same scene under fresh circumstances or between different characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetitions are more laughable the more complex and more naturally introduced the repeated scene is — the playwright must reconcile complexity and naturalness. Contemporary comedy often repeats a series of incidents act after act; classic examples include Moliere (L'Ecole des femmes, L'Etourdi, George Dandin) where one arrangement of events is repeated in three tempi. Repetition may occur with the same characters in new surroundings or with different groups (masters/servants), and can be used symmetrically to produce comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation or invert roles (e.g., a prisoner lecturing a magistrate, a child teaching parents), producing comedy by role reversal or by a plot in which the villain becomes the victim of his own villainy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inverted scene need not be shown in full if the audience can imagine the reversed counterpart; stock examples include the 'robber robbed' and instances where a trap laid by a character catches its author (Lawyer Pathelin). Inversion is widely used but considered the least interesting of the sentence-level devices compared with other transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it belongs simultaneously to two altogether independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at once (the stage-made misunderstanding is a particular case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key requires both independence and partial coincidence of the series. The author must continually recall the audience's attention to both the independence and the coincidence (renewing the threat of the partnership dissolving); examples include equivocal misunderstandings, past vs present series forced to coincide (Daudet's Tartarin manacled to Bonivard) and Labiche's plays that build separate series and then make them interfere. The comic arises more from exposing the interference than from mere equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life (absentmindedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light comedy aims to 'mechanise' life — to present actions and relations as repeatable, reversible, and interchangeable, turning natural continuity into a jointed, mechanical spectacle; absentmindedness in events or persons is the root of the ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy exaggerates the incidental rigidity or absentmindedness found in life. Treat life as a repeating mechanism (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) to obtain comic effect. Absentmindedness is an 'incurable' source of laughter and is the basis for constructing artificial comic systems (theatre, farce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between comic that is 'expressed' (can be translated across languages/societies) and comic 'created by language' (owing entirely to sentence structure or word choice and generally untranslatable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic created by language depends on lapses or particularities of a language (word order, gendered words, idioms) and often cannot be transferred without loss; this category includes puns, word-play, and devices that exploit the structure of language itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty (esprit) vs Comic (in speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is comic when it makes us laugh at the person who utters it; witty (spirituel) when it makes us laugh at a third party or at ourselves. Wit is the comic in a highly volatile, condensed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit often functions by quickly evoking a comic scene in miniature; to analyse wit, expand the remark into a regular scene and identify which comic category (repetition, inversion, interference) it corresponds to. Wit presupposes a dramatic way of thinking — seeing ideas converse as persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for analysing/producing wit: expand remark into scene
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyse a witty remark, enlarge it into a regular scene and identify which category of the comic the scene belongs to; this reduces wit to its comic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mme. de Sévigné's 'Your chest hurts me' expands into a Moliere scene (the sham doctor diagnosing a daughter from the father). For creation, craft a compact remark that evokes a larger comic situation by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity fitted into a well-established phrase-form
rubrics_metrics.description: A COMIC MEANING IS INVARIABLY OBTAINED WHEN AN ABSURD IDEA IS FITTED INTO A WELL-ESTABLISHED PHRASE-FORM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect arises when a ready-made phrase is completed with an absurdity that reveals automatism. Examples: M. Prudhomme's sayings (e.g. 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie'), or dovetailing two commonplace sayings to slip an absurd meaning past the ear (Labiche). The absurdity itself isn't the source of comedy but makes the automatism obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalization of metaphor / physical vs moral meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is obtained when an expression used figuratively is deliberately taken literally, i.e., attention is diverted to the physical/material meaning when the moral/figurative is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Tous les arts sont freres' made comic by focusing on 'frere' materially or by altering gender ('Tous les arts sont soeurs'). Rejoinders that force a concrete image from a figurative phrase (sport metaphors, literal continuations) produce witty rejoinders and laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of meanings (word-play and puns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring two independent meanings into the same expression so the sentence supports two sets of ideas simultaneously; the play upon words exploits different meanings (especially figurative vs literal) to reveal a lapse in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are the crudest form (homophony producing two different sentences); higher forms present one sentence with two legitimate interpretations. The play upon words often feels like a negligence of language and is amusing because it temporarily makes language accommodate things to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion at sentence-level
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment by reversing syntactic roles (putting subject in place of object and vice versa) to obtain a comic meaning or refutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common device among wits (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' -> 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?'). Considered less substantial than interference or transposition but easy to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (comic transformation of sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer ideas into a different stylistic key or environment while preserving their mutual relations (the linguistic analogue of repetition); by placing ideas in an unfamiliar style the language itself becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposition is a far-reaching device: one shows only the transposed expression and relies on the audience to supply the 'natural' one. This is analogous to repetition in action-based comedy and is especially powerful when the audience instinctively supplies the original register or style that is being parodied or displaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appearance of likelihood / prepare audience acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Even extraordinary coincidences or mechanical treatments must preserve an aspect of likelihood; contemporary comedies often secure acceptance by preparing the audience gradually so an unlikely repetition or coincidence becomes acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two approaches: contemporary authors mesmerise the audience (prepare them) so acceptance creates the effect; classical authors make repetition seem natural through consistent character forces (comedy of character). The playwright must choose technique appropriate to desired naturalness (audience-conditioning vs intrinsic character logic).
